newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil, Argentina patch up spats, sign deals.
newsitem.headline: Brazil, Argentina patch up spats, sign deals.

text.p: Brazil and Argentina on Sunday patched up a series of disputes, striking deals on car imports and signing accords on border controls and military cooperation.

Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso and his Argentine counterpart Carlos Menem said after meeting in Rio de Janeiro that despite disagreements, there were no problems between the two countries that could not be resolved.

In addition, while speaking of "solid friendship" and "perfect convergence of opinion", the presidents said the South American trade bloc Mercosur, which groups Brazil, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, was doing fine and would continue to grow.
"There has never been an issue that has not been resolved through political understanding," Cardoso said.

Menem flew to Rio on Saturday for a one-day summit with the Brazilian leader, billed by Brazilian Foreign Ministry officials as just another in a series of regular meetings between the heads of Mercosur's two most important economies.

Argentine newspapers have reported that the talks were crucial in determining the future of Mercosur because of Argentine anger at Brazilian car industry policy and recent restrictions on import financing, among other gripes.

At a meeting opened to the media between ministers of both governments in Rio's Copacabana Palace Hotel, Argentine Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella dismissed reports that "used words which do not correspond at all to reality, like conflict".
The two countries on Sunday signed a deal allowing car makers based in Argentina to export some 110,000 vehicles to Brazil over the next three years.

The deal was a concession to Buenos Aires, which has been railing at a Brazilian presidential decree offering generous tax breaks to auto manufacturers who establish factories in the impoverished northeast.
As for the import finance dispute, officials said both sides had agreed to meet again in several months to discuss it further.
Cardoso, Menem and their ministers on Sunday signed accords on allowing private firms to run ferries across rivers on the border, on border control integration and on military cooperation.
They also agreed that Brazil would buy up 1,000 megawatts of excess Argentine electricity and to beef up cross-border infrastructure such as bridges.
Perhaps most importantly, Brazil agreed to consult its southerly neighbor more regularly over macroeconomic policy.

Brazil's move to limit short-term import financing at the end of last month caught its Mercosur partners totally by surprise, infuriating the other governments and even leading to a charge of "treason" from the Argentine envoy to Brasilia.
The Brazilian leader also reaffirmed Brasilia's support for Buenos Aires' bid to host the 2004 Olympics, now that Rio had failed to make the shortlist.
